name: Straw
lede: Straw is the pale yellow of dried grain stalks, named for the stalks themselves and listed in chart after chart of color names since the sixteenth century.

sections.title: A color named for the stalk
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary glosses *straw* as yellow and *straw-coloured* as the pale yellow of straw [1]. It also keeps two older adjectives: *stramineous*, simply straw-coloured, and *festucine*, a greeny-yellow straw [1]. *Light straw* is the color of white wine [1]. The Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 dates the English color name to 1589 [14].

In printed English the adjective *straw* rose fastest in the 1840s and peaks in the 1870s [16]. The two-word phrase *straw yellow* peaks much later, around the 1920s, at a far smaller frequency [16].

The swatch here, #E4D96F, is a clear greenish yellow, which ISCC-NBS calls light greenish yellow, with CIELAB chroma 54 [14]. That is stronger than the word suggests. The xkcd survey's straw is a paler #FCF679, and the nearest names to our swatch are [[dull-yellow]], [[sandy]] and [[khaki]] [14].

sections.title: Werner's straw yellow
sections.body:
In the Werner and Syme nomenclature, Straw Yellow is no. 71, between Honey Yellow and Wine Yellow [2]. Its recipe is sulphur yellow, a large share of greyish white and a touch of ochre yellow [2]. That recipe describes a pale, greyish yellow, where our swatch is a saturated greenish one [2][14]. The examples were oat straw among plants, the fur of the polar bear among animals and calamine among minerals [2].

The recipe starts from [[sulphur-yellow]], which makes straw a diluted yellow, not a separate hue. In the lab, a precipitate of antimony sulphide passes from straw-yellow through lemon-yellow and orange-red to deep crimson as the conditions change [13].

sections.title: Straw in cloth, hats and steel
sections.body:
[[leghorn]] is the yellow of straw, named for Livorno, whose wheat gave the straw for Leghorn hats; the straw was harvested green and bleached before it was used [1]. *Tuscan-coloured* also meant straw-coloured [1].

Dyers and drapers used the word plainly. The V&A describes one Kashmir shawl fragment as straw, saxe blue, green muscat, claret and mole on a saffron ground [10]. Furetière's French dictionary distinguished five shades of yellow, putting straw (*paillé*) between lemon and golden [7]. French fabrics sold as Nankin yellow, fashionable from the 1740s to the 1770s, ran from light yellow nearly to orange and took in blond, straw, buff and beige tones; the name was a marketing device [8].

Straw is also a heat color. Straw-coloured is one of the colors steel takes on when heated, and it marks the stage where the steel has been annealed and is less brittle [1]. Farrow and Ball's off-white String was first named Straw Left out in the Rain by the paint designer John Fowler in the 1930s [11].

One old misreading is worth correcting. In old novels, *tow-headed* does not mean hair that sticks up like straw. Tow is the lower-quality flax used for rope and coarse cloth, and tow-headed hair has its dirtier goldish color [10].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body:
The yellows on Paleolithic cave walls leaned toward orange, beige and brown, and never toward green or lemon [3]. Pastoureau lists them from the lightest, straw, through chamois, apricot and honey, down to russet, tawny, bister and bronze [3]. Our swatch leans green, which none of them did.

Medieval heraldry treated shade as unimportant. A yellow could be lemon, straw, honey or mustard, and what counted was the idea of yellow [4]. Straw could still decide an argument: the straw-yellow dress of a young woman in a Florentine portrait, painted with massicot and [[flower:weld|weld]] lake, led to the picture being given to Alessio Baldovinetti and taken from Piero della Francesca [5].

From the 1560s until the Impressionists, true yellow grew scarce in painting and drifted toward browns, greens, greys, ochres, pinks, and straw or ivory tones [6]. In Italy, ivory, beige, straw, russet and light brown replaced yellow and allowed stronger contrasts, which Caravaggio used in Rome [6].

Straw also works as a foil. Nelson describes the male satin bowerbird dancing on a stage of shiny yellow grass, where the contrast between the yellow straw and his blue objects helps decide whether females visit [12].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 31 works [15]. They cluster in the late 1800s: 20 of 8,345 paintings from that century, and 9 of 1,173 from the 1890s, 5.9 times the archive's rate [15]. The strongest case is Indian painting: 11 of 721 Indian works match, and 7 of 96 Kalighat pictures from Calcutta [15].

The largest areas are Kalighat paintings of about 1890: the snake goddess Manasa, where the color fills 69 per cent of the canvas, and Hanuman attacking Indrajit, at 49 per cent [15]. In Europe the best case is [[painter:emile-bernard|Émile Bernard]]'s *La Moisson* of 1888, at 44 per cent [[painting:commons-Q17492114|The Harvest]] [15].

With the finer lens, the color first appears in 1434, in a work by [[painter:fra-angelico|Fra Angelico]], 155 years before the 1589 date given above for the name [15]. That is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of a dye. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 68 per cent of 69 paintings, and [[khaki]] turns up on the same canvases about 20 times more often than chance [15]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors.

Where to look: ripe grain, a woven hat or dry grass in low light, and compare it with the swatch. Real straw is usually paler and greyer.

openers: Werner's straw yellow was sulphur yellow mixed with much greyish white: a washed-out yellow, not a bright one.
Old novels' 'tow-headed' children are not straw-haired: tow is the coarse flax used for rope.
